abstract: >
  Existing large-area photovoltaic (PV) inventories resolve where solar
  installations are, but not how they are built. We present `pv_geom`, an
  open Python package that enriches a vector inventory of PV polygons with
  per-installation geometry derived from co-temporal classified airborne
  LiDAR: panel tilt and azimuth with bootstrap uncertainties, the orientation
  of the underlying roof plane, panel--roof angle, heights above ground and
  roof, and a rules-based mounting-type classification with per-row
  confidence and provenance. The pipeline is tile-centric and horizontally
  scalable: polygons are grouped by LiDAR tile, each tile group is processed
  independently on a Dask cluster (locally or on ephemeral cloud workers via
  Coiled), and results are written incrementally with per-group failure
  tolerance and crash-safe resume. Runs are reproducible bit-for-bit across
  backends via config hashing and per-polygon deterministic random seeds.
  We validate the method on metropolitan Phoenix, Arizona (~10 pts/m^2 USGS
  3DEP LiDAR): on a 1,000-polygon utility-scale benchmark, all fits succeed
  with inlier RMSE of 1.3 cm (median), and local and cloud backends produce
  identical output; a 8,906-polygon mixed-density stress test completes in
  25 minutes on 8 workers and demonstrates that the quality-flag system
  correctly isolates the long tail of small, sparse, or noisy input polygons
  rather than emitting unreliable fits. We discuss calibration and validation
  steps required before a metro-scale release.
keywords: [solar photovoltaics, LiDAR, RANSAC, plane fitting, mounting classification, distributed computing]

# Introduction

Large-area PV inventories built from aerial or satellite imagery — e.g.
DeepSolar for the United States [@yu2018deepsolar], a harmonised open dataset
for the UK [@stowell2020uk], and a global inventory of utility-scale units
[@kruitwagen2021global] — resolve the *presence*, *extent*, and rough
*capacity* of solar installations. What they do not resolve is *geometry*:
the tilt and azimuth of the modules, whether they are flush-mounted on a
pitched roof or racked above a flat one, whether a ground-mounted array is
fixed or tracking, and how the panels relate to the structure beneath them.

Geometry matters for several downstream questions:

1. **Yield modeling.** Tilt- and azimuth-aware irradiance transposition is
   the difference between assuming every rooftop system faces south at
   latitude tilt and modeling the fleet that actually exists.
2. **Mounting-type classification.** Flush-mount residential, tilted
   commercial rack, carport, fixed ground mount, and single-axis tracker have
   different cost structures, capacity densities, and policy relevance.
3. **Equity and policy analysis.** Fused with parcel and demographic data,
   installation geometry sharpens questions about who adopts which kind of
   system — the level of detail currently available only from permit records
   such as Tracking the Sun [@barbose2023tts], which cover a nonrandom subset
   of jurisdictions.
4. **Expansion headroom and shading.** Roof-plane orientation and
   panel--roof geometry are inputs to estimating remaining usable roof area.

Airborne LiDAR resolves this geometry directly. Where a LiDAR acquisition is
roughly co-temporal with the imagery underlying a polygon inventory, the
returns inside each PV polygon sample the panel surface itself, and the
returns around it sample the roof or ground beneath. `pv_geom`
operationalizes this observation at metropolitan scale: given a polygon
inventory, a classified LAZ tile archive on S3, and a building-footprint
layer, it produces a polygon-keyed attribute table with per-row quality flags
and full provenance.

The package is deliberately metro-agnostic — all thresholds, coordinate
systems, and point-classification conventions are configuration — and its
first deployment target is metropolitan Phoenix, Arizona: a ~417,000-polygon
PV inventory derived from a segmentation model applied to aerial imagery,
paired with the USGS 3DEP Maricopa--Pinal 2020 LiDAR collection
[@usgs3dep] at ~10 pts/m^2.

# Data {#sec-data}

**PV polygons.** A GeoParquet inventory of PV installation polygons with a
unique `polygon_id`. For Phoenix we use an atlas of 416,976 polygons produced
by a SAM-based segmentation pipeline over 2024 aerial orthoimagery
(median polygon ~11 m^2). MultiPolygons are exploded into single parts with a
`parent_polygon_id` link; the link column is carried through to the output, so
part-level rows can be aggregated back to input detections by grouping on it.
Polygons are reprojected once at ingest into the
LiDAR CRS (Phoenix: EPSG:6341, NAD83(2011) / UTM 12N, metres).

**LiDAR.** Classified LAZ tiles with a sidecar tile index. The Phoenix
archive (USGS LPC AZ MaricopaPinal 2020 B20) comprises 13,373 indexed
1-km tiles, of which 3,381 are currently mirrored to S3; delivered density is
9--11 pts/m^2. A practical complication: these tiles carry ASPRS classes 1
(unclassified), 2 (ground), and 7 only — there is no class 6 ("building").
`pv_geom` therefore supports a configurable fallback: when class 6 is absent,
panel/roof candidate points are class-1 returns more than a configurable
height (default 1.5 m) above the tile-group ground median.

**Building footprints.** FEMA USA Structures polygons for Arizona
[@femastructures]. Roughly 92% of atlas polygons intersect at least one
footprint; the remaining ~8% sit in genuine FEMA coverage gaps and surface in
the output as `on_building = False` (a data limitation we return to in
@sec-limitations). The FEMA `shape_area` attribute is unusable (all zeros in
this extract); areas are always recomputed from geometry.

# Methods {#sec-methods}

## Panel-plane fitting {#sec-panelfit}

For each polygon, panel-class returns are clipped to the polygon eroded
inward by 0.15 m (suppressing racking-edge and roof returns at the boundary),
and a plane is fit by RANSAC [@fischler1981ransac] with an inlier distance
threshold of 0.05 m and 200 iterations, followed by a least-squares
refinement (PCA: the plane normal is the smallest-variance right singular
vector of the centered inlier cloud), re-classification of inliers against
the refined plane, and RMSE computation on the final inlier set.

With unit normal $\hat{n} = (n_x, n_y, n_z)$ canonicalized to the upper
half-space ($n_z \ge 0$), tilt and compass azimuth follow as

$$
\theta_{\text{tilt}} = \arccos(n_z), \qquad
\phi_{\text{az}} = \operatorname{atan2}(n_x, n_y) \bmod 360^\circ ,
$$

with azimuth reported as NaN below a 1° tilt floor, where the direction a
near-horizontal panel "faces" is numerically and physically ill-defined.

A fit is attempted whenever at least 3 points survive clipping, but rows are
flagged `low_density` below 3 pts/m^2 or 30 points, and `poor_fit` when the
RANSAC consensus covers less than 60% of clipped points. The 30-point floor
is empirical: a bootstrap size-sweep on clean Phoenix panels showed tilt
estimates are *unbiased* down to N=5 with precision scaling as $1/\sqrt{N}$,
so the practical floor is not statistical noise but RANSAC's ability to
reject overshoot and multi-plane contamination, which requires roughly 30
inliers. At Phoenix densities that corresponds to ~3 m^2 — about the bottom
10--15% of atlas polygons.

**Uncertainty.** 1-σ uncertainties for tilt and azimuth are estimated by a
50-sample nonparametric bootstrap over the inlier set, refitting each
resample by PCA. Azimuth dispersion uses the Mardia circular standard
deviation $\sigma = \sqrt{-2 \ln R}$, where $R$ is the mean resultant length
[@mardia2000directional], avoiding the wrap-around artifacts of a naive
standard deviation on angles.

## Multi-plane detection {#sec-multiplane}

East--west racking on flat commercial roofs produces two panel populations
facing ~180° apart. After the primary fit, a second RANSAC pass runs on the
primary's non-inliers (looser 0.10 m threshold); if the secondary plane
captures at least 20% of the polygon's points, both planes are reported, and
the row is flagged `east_west_rack` when the two azimuths are within 25° of
opposite and tilts agree within 5°.

## Roof-plane extraction {#sec-roofplane}

To characterize the surface *beneath* a rooftop system, `pv_geom` fits a
plane to panel-class returns in a ring buffer around the polygon: the polygon
buffered outward (starting at 3 m), minus the polygon itself, minus any other
PV polygons on the same building, intersected with the chosen building
footprint (the intersecting footprint with maximum overlap). If fewer than
100 returns fall in the ring, the buffer expands in 0.5 m steps to a 5 m cap
before giving up with flag `roof_insufficient` — the common failure mode when
panels occupy most of the roof. A fit whose inlier RMSE exceeds 0.10 m is
rejected as `roof_complex` (dormers, hips, multi-facet bleed). From the panel
and roof fits together we derive the panel--roof angle (angle between the two
normals) and height-above-roof (vertical offset of the panel inlier centroid
from the roof plane).

## Heights {#sec-heights}

Height-above-ground is the median panel-inlier elevation minus the median
class-2 (ground) elevation within 10 m of the polygon centroid. When the
class-6 fallback is active (@sec-data), the ground reference for the
*candidate filter* is a single tile-group-wide ground median — defensible on
Phoenix's flat terrain at the 1-km tile scale, and revisit-worthy in
higher-relief metros.

## Mounting classification {#sec-mounting}

Mounting type is assigned by an ordered rules engine over the features
`(on_building, panel_tilt, panel_roof_angle, height_above_roof,`
`height_above_ground, area, aspect_ratio, roof_plane_available,`
`roof_tilt, east_west_rack)`. Rules are evaluated most-specific-first; the
first rule to clear a confidence of 0.5 fires. Each threshold comparison maps
to a confidence via a piecewise-linear ramp — 0.5 exactly at the threshold,
1.0 at a fractional margin (default 50% of the threshold) past it — and a
rule's confidence is the minimum over its clauses. Polygons matching no rule
are `ambiguous` with confidence $1 - \max(\text{near-miss confidences})$.

| Rule | Label | Core predicate |
|:----:|:------|:---------------|
| R7 | `east_west_rack_rooftop` | on building, EW two-plane signature, tilt ≤ 20°; if a roof fit exists it must be flat (guards against gable facets, which also face ~180° apart) |
| R1 | `flush_mount_pitched_roof` / `flush_mount_flat_roof` | on building, panel--roof angle ≤ 5°, height above roof ≤ 0.5 m; label splits on roof tilt vs 7° |
| R2 | `tilted_rack_rooftop` | on building, panel--roof angle > 5° and height above roof ≤ 1.5 m (or, without a roof fit: tilt > 5° and height above ground > 2.5 m) |
| R8 | `pole_mount` | off building, height ≥ 2 m, area ≤ 20 m^2, aspect ≤ 2 |
| R3 | `carport` | off building, height ≥ 2 m, aspect ≥ 2 |
| R4 | `ground_mount_tracker_suspected` | off building, height < 2 m, aspect ≥ 4, tilt < 35° |
| R5 | `ground_mount_fixed` | off building, height < 2 m, tilt ≥ 5° |
| R6 | `ambiguous` | default |

: Mounting rules in evaluation order. Rule IDs are stable identifiers, not
evaluation order: R7 and R8 were added after the initial six and run before
the broader rules that would otherwise absorb their polygons. {#tbl-rules}

Thresholds are configuration, not code; the R7/R8 and flat/pitched-split
defaults are physically motivated but *uncalibrated* pending a labeled
validation sample (@sec-limitations). The classifier sits behind an abstract
interface so a learned model can replace the rules without touching the
pipeline; rules would then remain as a fallback and explanation layer.

## Quality flags and provenance {#sec-provenance}

Every row carries its quality flags (`low_density`, `poor_fit`,
`near_horizontal`, `east_west_rack`, `tracker_suspected`,
`roof_insufficient`, `roof_complex`), the contributing LiDAR tile IDs, the
package version, a SHA-256 hash of the fully-resolved configuration, and a
run ID. A JSON manifest per run records the resolved config, input URIs,
cluster spec, counts, and aggregate quality statistics. Reproducibility is
by construction: RANSAC and bootstrap seeds derive from a SHA-256 of the
polygon ID (process-stable, unlike Python's salted `hash()`), so identical
inputs and config produce identical output regardless of worker count,
scheduling order, or compute backend.

# Implementation and scaling {#sec-implementation}

LAZ I/O dominates cost, so the pipeline is *tile-centric*: each polygon is
assigned a primary tile (containing its centroid) plus the set of tiles its
geometry overlaps; polygons are grouped by primary tile; and each tile
group's fetch list expands to the union of overlapping tiles. One Dask task
[@rocklin2015dask] processes one tile group: fetch all tiles (with local
caching), split the point cloud by class once for the whole group, then clip
and fit per polygon. Only the primary group emits a polygon's row, so
tile-spanning polygons need no dedup pass and raw point clouds are never
shuffled between workers.

Three design decisions matter at atlas scale (~1,000--2,000 tile groups):

- **Incremental writes with per-group failure tolerance.** Each partition is
  written the moment its group completes; a failed group is recorded in the
  manifest rather than aborting the run, and `--resume` retries exactly the
  missing partitions. A single worker loss at hour 3 of a multi-hour run
  costs one group, not the run.
- **Slim task graphs.** Tasks embed only their group's tile URIs (not the
  13k-entry index), and a single client-side S3 LIST drops indexed tiles with
  no LAZ object (~75% of the Phoenix index) before dispatch, replacing
  thousands of worker-side 404 round-trips.
- **Bounded memory.** Class filtering is hoisted out of the per-polygon loop
  and the raw 4-column point array (~1.5 GB on dense tiles) is freed before
  fitting begins. Phoenix's densest tiles (~3,000 polygons, >50M points)
  still require 16 GiB workers.

The same code runs serially in-process (`--no-dask`), on a local
`distributed.LocalCluster`, or on ephemeral cloud workers provisioned by
Coiled in the data's AWS region, selected purely by configuration.

# Validation and benchmarks {#sec-results}

## Point-level spike validation

A pre-implementation spike on 29 randomly drawn Phoenix polygons
established that the data supports the method: 27/29 plane fits achieved
RMSE < 0.05 m; the tilt distribution was bimodal at 5--10° (flush-mount) and
18--22° (tilted rack); and azimuths concentrated at 150--230° (south to SSW)
with none facing north — physically correct for Arizona. On one polygon with
visible segmentation overshoot into a yard, RANSAC reduced RMSE from 0.377 m
(plain SVD fit) to 0.018 m by rejecting the 14% of returns off the panel
plane, confirmed by aerial overlay.

## 1,000-polygon benchmark (utility-scale cluster)

A 1 km^2 bounding box capturing a utility-scale plant (@fig-bench1k): 1,000
polygons across 2 tile groups, all fits successful, panel RMSE p50/p90 =
1.3/1.6 cm. Wall time was 322 s on a 2-worker local cluster and 414 s on
Coiled (the difference is ~90 s cluster spin-up, ~25 s worker package
install, and cold S3 reads), with **bit-for-bit identical** algorithm output
across backends. The classifier splits the plant into 617
`ground_mount_tracker_suspected` and 363 `ground_mount_fixed` — a known
weakness of the per-polygon tracker heuristic that installation-level
clustering is designed to repair (@sec-limitations).

![Six-panel review of the 1,000-polygon benchmark: (a) tilt vs azimuth,
(b) panel-fit RMSE against the 5 cm specification floor, (c) polygons over
2024 orthoimagery, (d) mounting-type counts, (e) confidence by mounting type,
(f) quality flags.](figures/bench_1k_review.png){#fig-bench1k}

## 8,906-polygon stress test (mixed density)

A 3 km × 3 km box spanning 8 tiles and the full quality range of the input
atlas, run on 8 Coiled workers (2 vCPU / 16 GiB): 24.8 min wall, all 8,906
rows emitted. Here the input long tail becomes visible: 68% of panel fits
succeed; 42% of rows carry `low_density`, 32% `poor_fit`, and 33% classify
as `ambiguous`. Critically, *successful* fits remain excellent (RMSE p50/p90
= 1.5/1.8 cm): the flag system is correctly refusing the small, sparse, and
segmentation-noisy polygons rather than emitting junk geometry on them. We
treat the flagged share as an honest property of the input inventory, to be
addressed by input-side repair (fragment clustering, adaptive erosion) rather
than by loosening fit acceptance.

# Limitations and planned work {#sec-limitations}

1. **Footprint gaps.** ~8% of polygons are off-building solely because FEMA
   lacks the structure, shunting true rooftop systems toward ground/carport/
   ambiguous rules. Planned: fall back to a second footprint source where
   FEMA is empty.
2. **Uncalibrated classifier thresholds.** All rule thresholds — especially
   the new R7/R8 and flat/pitched defaults — await calibration against a
   ~200-polygon aerial-verified label set, which will also resolve whether
   the 33% ambiguous rate in the stress test reflects miscalibration or
   genuinely uninformative inputs.
3. **Per-polygon tracker heuristic.** Trackers are detected per polygon
   (elongated, low, off-building, modest tilt); the 1k benchmark shows one
   plant split across two labels. Planned: installation-level clustering
   (grouping by centroid proximity and orientation coherence), which also
   enables site typing, row-spacing/GCR estimates, and repair of
   segmentation fragments by inheritance from the cluster fit.
4. **Fixed erosion.** The 0.15 m inward erosion consumes a large share of
   points on the smallest polygons and drives part of the `low_density`
   rate; erosion should scale with polygon size.
5. **External validation.** Tilt/azimuth/mounting accuracy will be
   quantified against permit and interconnection records (e.g., Tracking the
   Sun [@barbose2023tts]) for a Phoenix sample.
6. **Flat-terrain assumption in the class-6 fallback.** The tile-wide ground
   median used to select above-ground candidate returns is appropriate for
   Phoenix but should become slope-aware before deployment in high-relief
   metros.

# Software availability {#sec-availability}

`pv_geom` is a Python package (src layout, `pyproject.toml`) with a Typer
CLI, Pydantic-validated YAML configuration, 152 unit tests on synthetic
inputs, and a gated integration test against real Phoenix data. Source:
<https://github.com/JobTaminiau/pv_geom>. A tagged release with an archived
DOI (Zenodo) and license is in preparation; until then the repository URL is
the citable reference. LiDAR: USGS 3DEP / LPC [@usgs3dep], hosted under the
ASU NSF Phoenix collection. Building footprints: FEMA USA Structures
[@femastructures].
